name: DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide)

card.summary: A nine-amino-acid research peptide first reported in the 1970s to promote sleep; human evidence is small and old.
card.note: Not an approved drug in the US; long-term safety has not been established in clinical research.

quick.overview:
DSIP is a nine-amino-acid neuropeptide described in 1970s Swiss research after being isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits. It is sold as a research peptide and discussed online as a way to promote deep sleep.

The human literature consists of small studies from the early 1980s, and findings across animal and human work are described as conflicting. No study has examined it for appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: How DSIP works is not settled. Its gene and receptor have not been identified, and it is broken down quickly in plasma. Proposed mediators include serotonergic and NMDA-related pathways.
quick.risks: Safety and possible side effects of long-term use have not been established in clinical studies. Research peptides sold online are not regulated as approved medicines, so product content is not guaranteed.

lead: Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP), also called emideltide, is a neuropeptide with the amino acid sequence WAGGDASGE. It was reported by a Swiss group in the 1970s, who isolated it from the cerebral venous blood of sleeping rabbits [1].

In biohacking and looksmaxxing recovery discussion, DSIP is described as a research peptide claimed to promote deep sleep. A small human study from 1981 reported increased sleep after intravenous infusion in six volunteers [2], but later findings from animal and human work have been described as conflicting [1].
No published study has examined DSIP for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Research peptide; not a labelled approved drug in the US

paras: The gene, precursor and receptor for DSIP have not been identified [1]. Researchers have proposed involvement of the dorsal raphe nucleus and serotonergic mechanisms [3][4], and work in rats examined interactions with serotonergic agonists on body temperature [5].
DSIP degrades quickly in plasma and serum, with an in vitro half-life of about 15 minutes, and degradation and aggregation of the peptide and two analogs have been studied [1][6].

A 1981 double-blind crossover study in six healthy volunteers gave DSIP by slow intravenous infusion in the morning; subjects reported sleep pressure and total sleep time increased by a median of 59 percent over a 130-minute interval [2]. A 1981 report also examined the effect of synthetic DSIP on disturbed human sleep [7]. Studies in people with Alzheimer-type dementia and other conditions have measured DSIP-like immunoreactivity in cerebrospinal fluid [8].

Wikipedia notes conflicting findings across human and animal research and states that long-term safety has not been established in clinical studies [1]. No studies have examined DSIP for appearance outcomes.
Rat studies in 1981 and 1982 reported that repeated intravenous DSIP or its phosphorylated form changed the daily pattern of locomotor activity [9][10].
